title: Second-Order Bilevel Optimization with Accelerated Convergence Rates
claim: Our lazy second-order method matches or beats baselines in oracle-call efficiency, reaching lower error with fewer calls across initializations.
layout: 2 side-by-side line plots, shared legend style, one panel per initial point
description: Two side-by-side line plots compare optimization algorithms on log error (y-axis, logarithmic from about 1e-17 to 1e-1) against number of oracle calls (x-axis, 0 to 1200). The left panel is captioned 'Initial point (x1, y1)' and the right panel 'Initial point (x2, y2)'. Each panel has a legend with five methods: PRAGDA (red circles), iMCN (blue diamonds), GDA (yellow squares), MCN (green dashed stars) and LMCN (magenta dash-dot triangles). GDA drops quickly at first, then declines slowly and linearly in log scale across the whole range. The second-order methods stay flat at first, then fall sharply. LMCN reaches the lowest error at the fewest calls, about 470 in the left panel and about 360 in the right. Gridlines are light gray. The eye goes to the steep magenta curve ending first.
caption: Comparison of LMCN and baseline algorithms in terms of oracle calls under different initial points $(\fx_1,\fy_1)$ and $(\fx_2,\fy_2)$.
abstract: This paper studies second-order methods for nonconvex-strongly-convex bilevel optimization. We propose a novel fully second-order bilevel approximation method (FSBA) that achieves an iteration complexity of $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(Îµ^{-1.5})$ for finding the $(Îµ, \mathcal{O}(\sqrtÎµ))$ second-order stationary point of the hyper-objective function. Our results demonstrate that second-order methods can achieve an accelerated convergence rate than first-order methods in bilevel optimization. To address the heavy computational cost associated with the second-order oracle, we introduce a lazy variant of FSBA, called LFSBA, which reuses second-order information across several iterations. We prove that LFSBA exhibits better computational complexity than FSBA by a factor of $\sqrt{d}$, where $d$ is the dimension of the problem. We also apply a similar idea to nonconvex strongly-concave minimax optimization and propose the lazy minimax cubic-regularized Newton (LMCN) method with better computational complexity compared to existing second-order methods.
